assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection transformed international trade. It changed how we understand who exports, who invests abroad and how gains from trade arise through reallocation. The framework is now standard, and it spawned a large body of empirical and quantitative work. This is a clear shift in what we know and how we understand it.
assessment.attribution: The core is the Melitz (2003) model plus the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI. Helpman has a wider record in trade theory. Redding is credited in the list for quantitative extensions, but the foundational contribution is best captured by Melitz and Helpman.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades have passed. The empirical confirmation is extensive and the framework is embedded in policy evaluation and teaching, so it is mature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer a broader trade prize including Redding or Grossman, or one on quantitative trade (B044).
Credit is shared with the earlier Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum empirical work and with Hopenhayn-style selection models, which I cannot fully weigh from the list text.
I have not independently checked how recently trade has been recognised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the basis of modern monetary policy analysis in central banks. The Calvo pricing device, the Taylor rule and Woodford's synthesis of microfounded policy analysis changed both academic practice and institutional policy. The impact on practice is large.
assessment.attribution: The list credits eight names, so the attribution problem is real. Calvo (staggered pricing), Taylor (rules and staggered contracts) and Woodford (the unified framework, interest and prices) are the most distinct conceptual contributions. Gali, Christiano-Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler are also major but more clearly build on or extend the core.
assessment.maturity: Decades of use and evaluation, including testing in and after the financial crisis. The framework is mature, though still contested.
uncertainties: The three-name limit forces a choice that excludes Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler.
Persistent debate about whether the framework performed well after 2008 and in the post-pandemic inflation.
Adjacent macro prizes (2011 and 2022) raise a question about balance across the macro field.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Methods for estimating demand with differentiated products and for dynamic industry models turned industrial organisation into an empirical, structural field. They are also used in merger review, trade, health and many other settings. The combination of new measurement tools and wide application is strong.
assessment.attribution: The BLP demand estimation approach (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) is the clearest unit. Pakes also has the dynamic models (Ericson-Pakes) and related estimators. Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin have important but more distinct contributions, so a three-person prize on the demand-estimation core is defensible.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use, with very broad adoption in academia and in antitrust practice.
uncertainties: Seven credited names make the boundary of the prize contestable.
Whether the committee favours an IO prize that includes the empirical-entry tradition (Bresnahan-Reiss).
Some identification concerns remain about the structural assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The work documents how technology, tasks and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality. The China-shock papers showed persistent local effects, and the task-based approach changed thinking about technology and work. It is relevant to current policy debates on adjustment, including the question of what to do for people who lose their jobs.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock results (Autor, Dorn, Hanson) are a coherent trio. Katz's contribution on skill-biased change is earlier and also important, but he is credited elsewhere (B009). The tasks framework also owes a lot to Acemoglu, who has already been honoured, which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: The main papers date from 2003 to 2016 and the evidence has been debated and extended. The long-run persistence findings are well established, though interpretation still develops.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 laureate's work on technology and with the 2025 prize on growth and innovation.
Debate about the size and permanence of the trade shock effects.
Whether the task-based framework should be credited mainly to others.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The construction of long-run series on top incomes and wealth from tax records, and later distributional national accounts, changed what is known about inequality. It is a data-and-measurement achievement of the kind that rewards deep archival work, and it reset the research and policy agenda.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-income series, and Zucman extended the work to wealth and offshore holdings. Credit is shared among them and with Atkinson, who is deceased, and with collaborators. The theoretical interpretation (r > g) is more contested than the measurement.
assessment.maturity: The top-income work is two decades old and has been replicated across countries. The wealth and offshore estimates are newer and still debated.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes about wealth estimates and the treatment of taxes and transfers.
Saez also appears in B001, so the committee may consider whether a combined prize is sensible.
Risk that policy advocacy influences perceptions of the scientific contribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Misallocation research gave a quantifiable account of why total factor productivity and income differ across countries, linking micro data on firms to aggregate outcomes. It reshaped growth and development economics and shares the interest in understanding why growth differs.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the key paper. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) is a parallel contribution, and Restuccia has also worked on agriculture and productivity gaps. Other credit (Banerjee-Duflo, Jones) overlaps with an area already recognised.
assessment.maturity: About 15 years of replication and extension. Measurement issues are discussed, but the framework is widely used.
uncertainties: Concerns that measured misallocation partly reflects measurement error or unobserved adjustment costs.
The 2019 and 2025 prizes cover neighbouring development and growth topics.
Rogerson, not credited in the list, is a natural co-contributor.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: A unified body of work on how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. It brought political institutions into formal economic analysis with testable implications and empirical evidence, including through state capacity and the origins of fiscal states.
assessment.attribution: Persson-Tabellini and Besley are the leading names, and their synthesis books and papers are well recognised. Historical-political work overlaps with Acemoglu-Robinson, which was recognised in 2024.
assessment.maturity: Developed over three decades with extensive empirical testing. It is mature.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2024 institutions prize may reduce novelty.
Personal and institutional ties between the field and the Swedish economics community are disclosed but not adjudicated here.
The empirical identification of constitutional effects is imperfect.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kiyotaki-Moore showed how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks, a basic mechanism for credit cycles. It is a foundational model of financial frictions in macroeconomics and underlies much post-crisis analysis.
assessment.attribution: The central paper is Kiyotaki-Moore (1997), a clean two-person contribution. Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist (the financial accelerator) is related, but Bernanke has already been recognised and Gertler and Gilchrist are credited with later or complementary work.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of use, with strong influence on policy after 2008. It is mature.
uncertainties: Close proximity to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises.
The list-based credit does not clearly settle whether Gertler or Gilchrist should be included.
Empirical validation of the amplification mechanism is indirect.
